clue.text: Old Bob makes one cross is so choosy

parts.note: a bob was the old British shilling, abbreviated S
a voter elects someone by marking a cross on the ballot paper

explanation.surface: A grumpy old fellow called Bob gets cross with anyone because he is so fussy.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob is not a man: it is slang for the pre-decimal shilling, written S. 'Makes one cross' means votes, putting an X on a ballot.
explanation.definitionFit: To pick only certain things out of many is to be discriminating or choosy.

clue.text: Runs, in footwear, to get fish

indicators.note: the runs abbreviation is placed inside the footwear

parts.note: spats are cloth coverings worn over the shoe and ankle
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Someone runs in their shoes to fetch fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprats are small herring-like sea fish.

clue.text: Pub not closing. Edward found

indicators.note: not closing means the last letter is left off the word for the pub

parts.note: a local is one's neighbourhood pub
Ted is a familiar short form of Edward

explanation.surface: The pub stays open late, and Edward has been found there.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain one's 'local' is the nearby pub one regularly drinks at.
explanation.definitionFit: Located means discovered or tracked down, that is, found.

clue.text: To many a rumour add one about the state

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a crossword way of saying many
on dit, French for 'they say', is a piece of gossip or rumour
I is the Roman numeral for one
on means about or concerning

explanation.surface: Someone instructs a gossip to add one more tale about the government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'add' simply joins the pieces. ON DIT is a French phrase used in English for a rumour.
explanation.definitionFit: A condition is a state of being, as in good condition.

clue.text: Import a reaper, one to take every ear

parts.note: to spell is to signify or import, as in 'this spells trouble'
a binder is a reaping machine that also ties the cut corn into sheaves

explanation.surface: Someone brings in a harvesting machine that will cut every ear of corn.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all farming, but the ear in the definition is a listener's ear.
explanation.definitionFit: A spellbinder is a speaker who holds an audience enthralled, capturing everyone's attention.

clue.text: Margaret Fair-of-face get your gun!

parts.note: the nursery rhyme says Monday's child is fair of face, so the phrase is Monday's, shortened to MON'S
Meg is a familiar short form of the name Margaret

explanation.surface: Someone calls to a pretty woman named Margaret, urging her to fetch her firearm, as in Annie Get Your Gun.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme 'Monday's child is fair of face' turns the hyphenated phrase into MON'S. MONS MEG is a famous medieval cannon kept at Edinburgh Castle.
explanation.definitionFit: Mons Meg is a huge fifteenth-century siege cannon, a celebrated piece of artillery.

clue.text: Drive is up. Ruin!

indicators.note: in a down entry, is up means the word is written from bottom to top

parts.note: to ram is to drive or force, as in ram home

explanation.surface: Two exclamations: the car journey is over, and disaster follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To mar something is to spoil or damage it.

clue.text: Grow up in this land, Peter? -!

definitions.text: Grow up in this land, Peter? -!

parts.words: Grow up in this land, Peter? -!
parts.note: the boy who refused to grow up lived on an island, and his reply to the question is the first part of its name

explanation.surface: Someone asks Peter whether he will grow up here, and he answers emphatically.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Pan lives in Never Land and never grows up; the dash is his one-word reply.
explanation.definitionFit: Never means at no time, Peter Pan's answer and the start of his island's name.

clue.text: One's after a bird with an old rifle

indicators.note: after places the numeral following the bird's name

parts.note: the martin is a small bird of the swallow family
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone is hunting a bird with an antique gun.
explanation.walkthrough: The Martini-Henry was a Victorian British army rifle; the surface wants it to be a weapon of hunting, which it is.
explanation.definitionFit: The Martini-Henry was a nineteenth-century breech-loading rifle, often just called a Martini.

clue.text: Fancying some aid in crossword solving?

definitions.meaning: fancying means supposing or surmising without proof
solvers often fill a light by making an informed stab at it

explanation.surface: A solver admits to liking a bit of help with the crossword.
explanation.definitionFit: Supposing without certainty is conjecture, and conjecture helps fill many lights in a crossword.

clue.text: He tells a story in Capek's play

indicators.note: the story and its article sit within the title of the Czech play

parts.note: R.U.R. is Karel Capek's play which introduced the word robot
conte is a French word, also used in English, for a short tale

explanation.surface: A man narrates a tale from one of the Czech dramatist's works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He tells a story' reads as the definition, but only 'He tells' defines; 'a story' goes inside R.U.R., Capek's robot play.
explanation.definitionFit: A raconteur is a skilled teller of anecdotes, someone who tells stories.

clue.text: Unfinished churchman gets the rod

indicators.note: the church official's title loses its last letter, so it is left incomplete

parts.note: a verger is a church official who looks after the building

explanation.surface: A churchman whose work is incomplete receives the rod as punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets the rod' suggests a caning, but the rod is the definition: a verge is a staff of office.
explanation.definitionFit: A verge is a ceremonial staff or wand carried before a dignitary, a rod of office.

clue.text: Everyone's making a noise in the passage

definitions.text: Everyone's making a noise in the passage

parts.words: Everyone's making a noise in the passage
parts.note: in a musical score, a passage where every performer plays together is marked with the Italian word for all

explanation.surface: Noisy people are chattering in the corridor.
explanation.walkthrough: The passage is a stretch of music, not a corridor; the Italian marking for all players is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Tutti is Italian for all, marking a section where the whole orchestra plays.

clue.text: Birds soil parts of the fence

parts.note: land means ground or earth, soil
rails are the horizontal bars making up a fence

explanation.surface: Birds dirty the fence posts.
explanation.definitionFit: Landrails are corncrakes, a kind of bird of the rail family.

clue.text: Ease of manner with which poor Susan learnt

indicators.note: poor suggests badly done, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Poor Susan was taught social grace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with which' is a link; 'poor' rearranges SUSAN LEARNT.
explanation.definitionFit: Naturalness is unaffected, relaxed behaviour, an ease of manner.

clue.text: Governor's function isn't, oddly enough in high esteem!

indicators.note: the rearranged letters are placed within the word for high esteem

parts.note: admiration is high regard or esteem

indicators.note: oddly means in a strange way, so the letters of the short word are jumbled

explanation.surface: A grumbler says the governor's job is, strangely, not held in respect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly enough' looks like a comment on the grumble but signals the anagram, and 'in' places it; 'high esteem' is the container, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Governing or managing affairs is administration, the running of an organisation or state.

clue.text: A girl takes drink-start of good evening out

parts.note: Vera is a girl's name
gin is a spirit, a drink

indicators.note: start of means only the first letter of the following word is used

explanation.surface: A young woman has a drink at the beginning of a pleasant night out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'evening out' looks like a night on the town but means levelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Averaging means smoothing out differences to a mean, making things level.

clue.text: Take flight without a bit of minor irritation

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the escape word goes round the rest

parts.note: to flee is to run away, take flight

explanation.surface: Someone runs off without a trace of minor annoyance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' here means outside, not lacking.
explanation.definitionFit: A fleabite is figuratively a trivial annoyance or slight inconvenience.

clue.text: Counsel to counsel

parts.note: barristers, called counsel, address one another in court with a polite traditional phrase

explanation.surface: Advice passed to a lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: In British courts, a barrister refers to the opposing barrister as 'my learned friend'.
explanation.definitionFit: Barristers conventionally call each other by this courteous term in court.

clue.text: Song about a hound in Sidney's work

indicators.note: about means the song's letters go round the other piece

parts.note: an aria is a solo song in an opera
a hound is a contemptible man, a cad

explanation.surface: A ballad about a dog appears in a poet's writings.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Philip Sidney was an Elizabethan poet whose prose romance is the Arcadia; 'hound' means a cad, not a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Sidney's Arcadia is a pastoral prose romance of the 1580s.

clue.text: Wander through badly teed round

indicators.note: the jumbled letters are placed round the word for through
badly means the letters of the golf word are disordered

parts.note: via means by way of, through

explanation.surface: A golfer strays across a poorly teed-up round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' looks like a round of golf beside 'teed', but it is the container signal; 'badly' gives DETE.
explanation.definitionFit: To deviate is to stray from a course, to wander.

clue.text: Readily flowing — in a speakeasy context

definitions.meaning: smooth and effortless, as a stream or prose may be
read as speak easy, it means able to talk a language without effort

explanation.surface: Drink flows freely in an illicit bar.
explanation.definitionFit: Fluent describes both smooth flow and effortless speech, so both senses fit.

clue.text: Traditional, turbulent Lancaster

indicators.note: turbulent means disordered, so the city name's letters are stirred up

explanation.surface: The northern English city of Lancaster has a stormy, time-honoured history.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ancestral is handed down from forebears, hence customary or traditional.

clue.text: The first numbers in confusion

parts.note: the idiom for disorder pairs two numbers, and this clue wants the first of the pair

explanation.surface: Early figures are all muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sixes and sevens' means in confusion.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom at sixes and sevens means in disarray; this plural is its first half.

clue.text: .The block for the shoemaker

parts.note: the shoemaker is a farrier who shoes horses, and the block is the iron one he hammers on

explanation.surface: A cobbler's last on his workbench.
explanation.walkthrough: A cobbler is the obvious shoemaker, but a farrier, who shoes horses, works hot iron on this block.
explanation.definitionFit: An anvil is the heavy iron block a smith or farrier hammers metal on.

clue.text: A Prohibitive guide?

parts.note: the Catholic Church kept a famous list of forbidden books, a guide to what was prohibited

explanation.surface: A guidebook that forbids things.
explanation.walkthrough: The Index Librorum Prohibitorum was the Catholic Church's list of banned books; an index is also a guide to a book.
explanation.definitionFit: An index is a guide to contents, and the Index was the list of prohibited books.

clue.text: Quietly drink back — brewed tea, say

parts.note: P, piano, is the musical direction for playing quietly

indicators.note: the word for the drink is read from its end towards its start

parts.note: cider is an alcoholic drink made from apples

indicators.note: brewed suggests stirring up, so the letters of the hot drink are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone sips quietly, then puts the drink down, a pot of tea having been made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns CIDER into REDIC; 'brewed' rearranges TEA as ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To predicate is to state or affirm something, to say it is so.

clue.text: Flat stuff?

definitions.meaning: a slang word for an apartment or home
to stuff or fill out with soft material

explanation.surface: Something limp and squashed.
explanation.definitionFit: A pad is slang for one's home or apartment, and to pad is to fill out with wadding.

clue.text: Passed ! Might well pleased

indicators.note: might well suggests the letters could equally be in another order, so the last word is rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone who has just got through an exam might well be pleased.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might well' signals the anagram of PLEASED: its letters might well make another word.
explanation.definitionFit: Time that has elapsed has gone by, that is, passed.

clue.text: Gets upset-about: husbands, in part

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go round the men
upset means knocked over or disturbed, so the first word's letters are rearranged

parts.note: husbands are men

explanation.surface: Someone becomes distressed over husbands, at least partly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' looks like distress but is the anagram signal, giving SEGT; 'about' is the container signal and 'in' a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A segment is a portion or section of a whole.
